source.title: Analyzing Lottery Ticket Hypothesis from PAC-Bayesian Theory Perspective

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own experiments showing that lottery-ticket subnetworks’ test performance depends on learning rate, flatness, and distance from initialization, refining the generalization account for sparse subnetworks. It does not test the broad claim about memorizing arbitrary labels and generalizing on natural labels.
record.gate_note: Rows include the paper’s reported test-accuracy comparisons and measurements on winning tickets, label-noise settings, optimizers, regularizers, and PAC-Bayes formulations. Cited prior-work results are not rows. Hyperparameter selection details are not separate results. Figures 1, 3, 5, 6, and 7 are described in text but do not provide recoverable exact point values in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study investigates lottery-ticket subnetworks, learning rates, Hessian sharpness and PAC-Bayes formulations, but tests none of V1–V8. In particular, its unscaled Hessian and loss-landscape measurements do not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure or its ranking of generalization gaps. SAM and NVRM are SGD-based methods, not the adaptive optimizers named in V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: small-learning-rate IMP produces relatively sharp minima, distance from initialization matters for winning-ticket recovery, and the proposed spike-and-slab PAC-Bayes formulation qualitatively captures the observed behavior better than the tested zero-mean Gaussian formulation. The comparison changes both distribution structure and prior centering, so it does not isolate either factor. The authors also interpret IMP and continuous sparsification through PAC-Bayes and leave settings requiring early-epoch rewinding unanalyzed.
record.recipe_differences: The study follows the original IMP setting but analyzes sparse subnetworks and adds label-noise, sharpness-aware optimizer, distance-regularization, and PAC-Bayes experiments; it does not test the claim’s natural-label versus random-label memorization comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate and label noise; optimizer (SGD, SAM, NVRM); sparsity; regularization type and strength; model (ResNet20 or VGG16); dataset (CIFAR10 or CIFAR100); PAC-Bayes distribution/prior choice.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing learning rate can impair clean-data winning-ticket recovery while improving test accuracy under label noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning-rate effects on IMP subnetworks depend on label noise and sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM and NVRM lower Hessian trace relative to small-learning-rate SGD. Test accuracy improves in most reported settings, ties in two SAM settings, and decreases slightly in one NVRM setting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SGD-based sharpness regularization can flatten IMP solutions and improve their test accuracy, with setting-dependent results.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM does not recover winning tickets at large learning rates; distance-to-initialization regularization can, while ordinary L2 regularization lacks the same recovery trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Winning-ticket recovery depends on distance from initialization in addition to local flatness.

fits_no_version.finding: At small learning rates, sufficiently strong regularization widens the accuracy difference between sparse and dense networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization type and strength affect whether IMP recovers winning tickets.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors interpret the spike-and-slab formulation as better capturing test-accuracy groups than the zero-mean Gaussian comparator.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An initialization-centered spike-and-slab PAC-Bayes formulation can describe IMP generalization patterns better than the tested Gaussian formulation.

record.code_released: https://github.com/facebookresearch/open_lth (modified version used; repository cited in text)
record.problems: Several results are figure-only and have no exact numerical values in the supplied text. The label-noise fraction is not specified. Accuracy tables average over three runs but provide no uncertainty estimates. PAC-Bayes comparison is shown only for ResNet20 on CIFAR10 at 90% sparsity. Main empirical settings use CIFAR datasets and pruned networks, limiting transfer to dense networks or other data.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Figure-only plots were recorded only when the text explicitly describes the reported trend; precise values were unavailable.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels, natural-label generalization with the same recipe, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets and recovery recipes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions, small-data regimes, excessive dropout, and joint dropout/weight-decay removal with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus training–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus equal-sized random removals and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All rows are outside the supplied versions; cannot_determine therefore concerns claim applicability, not whether the reported numerical results are readable. Figure 2 additionally shows flatter large-learning-rate solutions with worse test accuracy and higher training loss, which does not challenge V7's specified measure and low-training-loss comparison. No omitted result tests a supplied version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not compare fitting arbitrary random labels with generalization on natural labels.
No sweep over network width or interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
The paper measures sharpness and test accuracy for pruned networks, but does not measure the magnitude-aware perturbation criterion or compare its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
